query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, the inherent multi‐principal element design promotes local chemical ordering and a high density of grain boundaries, which together enable the rapid formation of a continuous, chromium‐rich protective oxide (e.g., CrTaO4 or Cr2O3). This protective layer forms by preferential diffusion of Cr along grain boundaries while the overall sluggish bulk diffusion limits further cation migration. The result is an adherent, self-healing oxide scale that curbs both oxygen ingress and alloy element egress at high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: An equimolar high-entropy alloy (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi or similar) processed to exhibit an ultrafine-grained microstructure with substantial grain boundary density and local chemical ordering.
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA to an isothermal, high-temperature (approximately 1000°C) oxidative environment and perform a controlled comparison with a conventional alloy that has a similar concentration of oxide-forming elements but lacks the multi‐principal element design.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in air at 1000°C for an extended duration (e.g., ~200 hours) to allow scale development under identical thermal and atmospheric conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The high density of grain boundaries in the ultrafine-grained HEA, which acts as preferential pathways for chromium diffusion, and the local chemical ordering that biases selective oxidation.
generation.mechanism: In HEAs, the multi-element complexity results in both increased grain boundary diffusion channels (facilitating rapid Cr migration) and overall sluggish bulk diffusion (limiting excessive outward cation flow). This balance promotes the formation of a coherent, continuous Cr-rich oxide layer that acts as a barrier, thereby enhancing the alloy’s oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HEA will form a more uniform, adherent, and continuous Cr-rich protective oxide layer with lower overall weight gain during high-temperature exposure compared to the conventional alloy. This indicates improved oxidation resistance through both reduced inward oxygen diffusion and limited outward diffusion of alloying elements.
generation.baseline: A conventional alloy with a similar concentration of oxide-forming elements but without the multi‐principal element structure is expected to form a more heterogeneous, discontinuous mixed oxide (e.g., less continuous Cr-rich oxides mixed with less protective phases) and exhibit higher oxidation rates.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is anticipated to operate under high-temperature oxidation conditions (around 1000°C) and for alloys processed to high grain boundary densities. Its effectiveness may vary if the elemental makeup or processing conditions (e.g., grain size refinement) differ significantly from those specified.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative role of grain boundary density and local chemical ordering in promoting a protective Cr-rich oxide layer is supported by existing evidence, the precise contributions of individual elements (such as Ta when present) and the quantitative differences in oxidation kinetics remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the HEA with an ultrafine-grained microstructure and one set of a conventional alloy having a similar overall content of oxide-forming elements. Expose both sets to identical isothermal oxidation conditions at 1000°C in air for ~200 hours. Characterize the oxide scales using cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and X-ray diffraction (XRD), and measure the weight gain over time.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness, uniformity, and morphology
Chemical composition and elemental distribution within the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA does not develop a significantly more uniform, adherent, and continuous Cr-rich oxide scale (with lower weight gain and a clearer barrier to oxygen ingress) compared to the conventional alloy under identical conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi HEA was successfully fabricated through the arc-melting process, with an emphasis on phase, microstructure, and real-time oxidation behaviour in two different non-ambient (high-temperature and low-oxygen partial pressure) conditions. The main findings of this research work can be summarised as follows. In a vacuum (4.2 × 10−6 atm), only MnO, a halite-type oxide, was formed during in situ oxidation, contrary to ThermoCalc’s prediction of both halite and spinel oxides, and Ni/Co forming halite. In air (1.0 atm), vigorous oxidation was observed, with most of the oxides formed being spinel. Mn remained important in the formation of spinel oxides, and Co was predicted to form spinel oxides by ThermoCalc but was not found in oxide-forming elements. Oxides like Cr2O3, Fe2O3, and Fe3O4 were not detected during in situ HTXRD in either vacuum or air, which contrasts with previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. Mn was found to be a higher oxide-forming element, producing non-protective oxides, and leading to the depletion of Mn in the bulk alloy beneath the oxide layer. Such dependence is usually observed in either during the initial stage of oxidation or oxidation at relatively lower temperatures. cited_evidence.text: The order of formation of various metal oxides is governed by their thermodynamic properties, given by Gibbs free energy at a specific temperature. Al2O3 mainly forms as the bottom most oxide layer, due to its highest thermodynamic energy of formation (−903.88 kJ/mol of O2 at 850 °C) calculated using FactsageEdu73 software. Chromia, with the lowest standard free energy (−574.26 kJ/mol of O2 at 850 °C), forms the topmost oxide layer for the ultrafine-grained samples. Inner oxides are more likely to form in samples processed at high strain rate, since short circuit diffusion channels and high SFE sites are provided by the high intensity GBs present in the ultrafine-grained samples. These channels aid the inward flux of O ions to react with the metallic ions and form the internal oxides. The poor oxidation behavior of the as-cast samples is due to the formation of a nonadherent mixed oxide layer (spinel) above the alumina scale owing to the low diffusion of elements through GBs, which fails to restrict the accumulation of cations (M+) and anions (O2–) as reported in few previous studies as well. A coarse grain microstructure having BCC/B2 phases was obtained in the as-cast HEA sample. Only 5 min of straining of sample significantly refined the grain structure from 98 to 1 μm and 0.43 μm for the SFP_400 and SFP_1800 sample, respectively. The ultrafine-grained samples showed a phase transition from BCC/B2 to FCC structure. The SFP_400 sample showed a 12–20% reduction in the oxidation kinetics, whereas the SFP_1800 sample showed a 38–48% reduction in the oxidation kinetics compared to the as-cast alloy. Low values of parabolic rate constant and high values of activation energy for the ultrafine-grained samples show the high oxidation resistance of the processed samples. Protective oxide scales of Al2O3 and Cr2O3 were predominantly found after discontinuous isothermal oxidation. Other than protective scales, the availability of Co(Cr,Fe)2O4 spinel phases was also observed during the oxidation at elevated temperatures. The presence of more GBs favoring outward flux of elements to form a dense chromia layer followed by internal Al-rich oxide layered structure is responsible for the enhanced oxidation resistance of the processed samples.
